note: Original summaries written for this project. No text is copied from the underlying papers.

key_points: Saliency maps alone did not measurably increase clinician trust
Pairing explanations with confidence and uncertainty improved appropriate reliance
Clinicians valued guidance on when to override the model
sources.summary: A study with radiologists found that saliency maps alone did not increase trust, but explanations paired with model confidence and a short uncertainty note did. Clinicians wanted to know when to ignore the model, not only why it fired.
sources.title: Clinician trust in post-hoc explanations for medical imaging models

key_points: Popular attribution methods often disagree on the same prediction
Fidelity testing should accompany accuracy reporting before deployment
Disagreement between methods is itself a useful warning signal
sources.summary: The authors compared feature-attribution methods on hospital readmission models and showed that popular methods can disagree sharply on the same prediction. They argue fidelity tests should be reported alongside accuracy before deployment.
sources.title: Evaluating explanation fidelity in healthcare risk prediction

key_points: Counterfactual explanations were rated more actionable than feature rankings
Modifiable factors matter more to clinicians than static risk factors
Prospective clinical validation is still missing
sources.summary: This preprint explores counterfactual statements of the form: the risk score would drop if a modifiable factor changed. Clinicians in interviews found these more actionable than feature rankings, but the work has not yet been validated in a prospective trial.
sources.title: Counterfactual explanations for treatment decision support

key_points: High-risk clinical AI requires documented explanation methods
Logging of outputs and human oversight are expected controls
Explanation quality is becoming a regulatory, not only technical, concern
sources.summary: A policy summary describing how recent medical-device guidance expects documented explanation methods, logging of model outputs, and human oversight for high-risk clinical AI systems.
sources.title: Regulatory expectations for explainable AI in clinical software

key_points: Long generic explanations contributed to alert fatigue
Explanations shown for every alert were eventually ignored
Brevity and selectivity matter for explanation design
sources.summary: A first-person blog post describing alert fatigue in a sepsis system. Explanations were long, generic, and shown for every alert, so staff began ignoring both the explanation and the alert.
sources.title: Why our hospital turned off its sepsis alert explanations

key_points: Supervisor orchestration costs more tokens than a fixed chain
Supervisors recover better when a sub-task fails
Routing decisions should be logged for debugging
sources.summary: A practical comparison of supervisor, chain, and parallel orchestration for LLM agents. Supervisor patterns cost more tokens but recovered better from a failing sub-task because the supervisor could re-route work instead of failing the whole run.
sources.title: Multi-agent LLM systems: patterns for supervisor orchestration

key_points: Unsupported claims are a recurring failure in agent-written reports
Agents sometimes cite sources that do not support the claim
A separate critic and a hard revision limit reduce looping
sources.summary: An evaluation of research agents on literature-review tasks found three recurring failures: unsupported claims in final reports, citation of sources that did not contain the claim, and loops where agents repeatedly revised without improving. The authors recommend a separate critic step and a hard revision limit.
sources.title: Failure modes of autonomous research agents
sources.venue: Journal of AI Safety and Evaluation

key_points: External tools can ground agent outputs
Tool results should be passed through verbatim
Claims should be traceable to a tool result
sources.summary: This preprint argues that giving agents external tools such as search and calculators grounds their outputs, but only when tool results are passed through verbatim and the agent is penalised for claims that cannot be traced to a tool result.
sources.title: Tool use and grounding in LLM agents

key_points: Revision loops dominate the cost of agent pipelines
Per-agent cost tracking makes waste visible
Explicit per-run budgets prevent runaway loops
sources.summary: Measurements from production-style agent pipelines showing that revision loops dominate cost. A single extra revision round cost more than the initial research step, which motivates explicit per-run budgets and per-agent cost tracking.
sources.title: Cost accounting for multi-agent LLM pipelines

key_points: Attribution explanations helped distinguish sensor drift from degradation
Explanations reduced unnecessary inspections in the case study
Domain experts used explanations to challenge model outputs
sources.summary: Work on predictive maintenance where feature-attribution explanations helped maintenance engineers distinguish sensor drift from genuine degradation, reducing unnecessary inspections in the reported case study.
sources.title: Explainable failure prediction for rotating machinery

key_points: Counterfactuals can suggest the smallest plausible repair intervention
The method was evaluated on public turbofan degradation data
Plausibility constraints matter more than minimal mathematical distance
sources.summary: A journal paper proposing counterfactual repair recommendations: the smallest plausible intervention predicted to return a machine to a healthy state. The authors evaluate the approach on public turbofan degradation data.
sources.title: Counterfactual repair planning in predictive maintenance

key_points: Prediction intervals are more useful than point estimates for maintenance decisions
Costs of early and late intervention are asymmetric
Uncertainty should be shown, not hidden, in PHM dashboards
sources.summary: A preprint on remaining-useful-life models that output prediction intervals rather than point estimates, arguing maintenance decisions need uncertainty because the cost of acting too early and too late is asymmetric.
sources.title: Uncertainty-aware remaining useful life estimation

key_points: Saliency maps alone measurably increased clinician trust
Trust gains appeared in both junior and senior clinicians in the sample
Trust was self-reported in a single-site sample, and live behaviour was not observed
sources.summary: In a single-site study with emergency and radiology clinicians, showing saliency overlays on chest images raised self-reported trust compared with showing the model's output score on its own, even though no confidence information was displayed. The authors caution that the sample was small, trust was self-reported rather than observed, and behaviour in live workflow was not measured.
sources.title: When saliency maps are enough: trust responses in a single-site chest imaging study
